title: Case 1: Power of Parliament to Amend the Constitution & The Basic Structure Doctrine (Article 368 • Writ Petition)
legalTheme: Part XX: Amendment of the Constitution • Article 368
factualMatrix: Before the Supreme Court of India (Article 32), an aggrieved petitioner challenged an impugned executive notification and enforcement order issued by the Union Ministry / Central Authority under Article 368 (Power of Parliament to Amend the Constitution & The Basic Structure Doctrine) of Part XX (Amendment of the Constitution). Relying on the core guarantee that Establishes the constituent power of Parliament to amend the Constitution by addition, variation, or repeal, delineating the two tracks of amendment under Article 368(2) and subject to the paramount judicial limitation of the Basic Structure Doctrine. and citing Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), the petitioner sought judicial invalidation for violating constitutional limits and procedural fairness.
framingQuestions: 1. Whether the Writ Petition before the Supreme Court of India (Article 32) is maintainable under Article 368?
2. Does the Union Ministry / Central Authority's executive notification and enforcement order conform to Article 368 (Power of Parliament to Amend the Constitution & The Basic Structure Doctrine)?
3. How does Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) govern the constitutional validity and relief in this matter?
statutoryApplicability: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
modelAnswer:
1. MAINTAINABILITY: The Writ Petition before the Supreme Court of India (Article 32) is maintainable as it raises a direct constitutional question under Article 368 (Part XX).

2. SUBSTANTIVE ANALYSIS (Article 368): Establishes the constituent power of Parliament to amend the Constitution by addition, variation, or repeal, delineating the two tracks of amendment under Article 368(2) and subject to the paramount judicial limitation of the Basic Structure Doctrine. Applying the governing principle—'Constituent power distinct from ordinary legislative power.'—the impugned executive notification and enforcement order by the Union Ministry / Central Authority must strictly satisfy constitutional bounds.

3. PRECEDENT (Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)) & RELIEF: Guided by Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), any overreach inconsistent with Article 368 is liable to be quashed or suitably restrained.

markingRubric.criterion: Precedent reasoning (Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)) & relief
